content: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have demonstrated that breastfeeding during painful procedures in newborns effectively reduces pain. The mechanisms behind this analgesic effect are thought to be multifactorial, involving the act of sucking, skin-to-skin contact, warmth, rocking, the sound and smell of the mother, and potentially the presence of endogenous opiates in breast milk. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effect of breastfeeding on procedural pain in infants aged 28 days to 12 months, compared to other interventions such as no treatment, placebo, parental holding, skin-to-skin contact, expressed breast milk, formula milk, bottle feeding, sweet-tasting solutions (e.g., sucrose or glucose), distraction, or other methods. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases up to February 18, 2016, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, as well as trial registries like ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The inclusion criteria were RCTs or quasi-RCTs involving infants aged 28 days to 12 months who were breastfed during painful procedures. Comparators included interventions such as oral water, sweet-tasting solutions, expressed or formula milk, pacifiers, positioning, cuddling, distraction, topical anesthetics, and skin-to-skin care. The procedures studied included subcutaneous or intramuscular injections, venipuncture, intravenous line insertion, heel lance, and finger lance. No language restrictions were applied. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were used for data collection and analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The primary outcomes were behavioral or physiological indicators of pain and composite pain scores. Data were pooled for comparable outcomes when at least two studies provided relevant data. Mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for continuous outcomes measured on the same scale, while standardized mean differences (SMDs) were used for outcomes measured on different scales. Risk ratios (RRs) were planned for dichotomous outcomes, but insufficient data prevented pooling of these outcomes. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, and a 'Summary of findings' table was created. The review included 10 studies with a total of 1,066 infants, all of which were conducted during early childhood immunizations. Due to the nature of the intervention, blinding of participants and personnel was not possible, leading to a high risk of bias in this domain across all studies. Nine studies were rated as having a low risk of bias for incomplete outcome data, but most studies had unclear risk of bias for random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and selective reporting due to insufficient information. Breastfeeding was found to reduce behavioral pain responses, such as cry duration and pain scores, during vaccination compared to no treatment, oral water, and other interventions like cuddling, oral glucose, topical anesthetics, massage, and vapocoolant sprays. However, breastfeeding did not consistently reduce physiological indicators of pain, such as changes in heart rate. Data from six studies (547 infants) showed that breastfeeding reduced cry duration by an average of 38 seconds compared to water or no treatment (MD -38 seconds, 95% CI -50 to -26; P < 0.00001). The quality of evidence for this outcome was rated as moderate, as most infants were younger than six months, and the results may not be generalizable to older infants undergoing 12-month immunizations. Pain scores from five studies (310 infants) showed a 1.7-point reduction in standardized pain scores with breastfeeding (SMD -1.7, 95% CI -2.2 to -1.3). This evidence was also rated as moderate quality for the same reasons. Heart rate data following injections were available from only two studies (186 infants), and the evidence was considered low quality due to insufficient data. No significant differences in heart rate were observed between breastfeeding and control groups (MD -3.6, 95% CI -23 to 16). Four of the 10 studies included more than two intervention arms. Breastfeeding was more effective in reducing crying duration and pain scores during vaccination compared to interventions such as 25% dextrose, topical anesthetic cream (EMLA), vapocoolant sprays, maternal cuddling, and massage. None of the included studies reported adverse events associated with breastfeeding during painful procedures. In conclusion, based on the 10 studies included in this review, breastfeeding appears to reduce pain during vaccinations in infants beyond the neonatal period. It consistently reduced behavioral pain responses, such as cry duration and composite pain scores, during and after vaccinations. However, there was no evidence to suggest that breastfeeding affected physiological pain responses. The review did not include studies involving hospitalized infants undergoing other skin-breaking procedures, so the findings may not be directly applicable to this population. Further research is needed to evaluate the efficacy, feasibility, and acceptability of breastfeeding as a pain management strategy in hospitalized infants.
